passage: "Saurabh, I went back to our old flat in Kolkata last week. Just stood outside. The building's been painted this weird green. The mango tree where we tied the cricket stumps is gone. And the tea stall uncle still recognised me! He said, 'Arnab babu, you've grown a beard.' I laughed and then had to turn away because my eyes were stinging. I kept thinking of summers when the only worry was whose turn it was to bat. Now it's rent, exams, job forms, Ma's health. Part of me wants to go back to being that nine-year-old, just for a day. But then I remember I also hated being told what to do all the time. It's weird. I miss it, and I'm glad it's over."

qa.q: What had happened to the mango tree outside Arnab's old flat?
qa.a: It was gone.

qa.q: Why did Arnab have to turn away at the tea stall?
qa.a: Being recognised brought back memories of his carefree childhood, and he felt a sudden rush of longing that made his eyes sting.

qa.q: What could Arnab do with this feeling instead of just aching?
qa.a: He could share memories with old friends like Saurabh or make small time for play, letting nostalgia comfort him without pulling him backward.

qa.q: How might the tea stall uncle have felt seeing Arnab again?
qa.a: He was probably happy and a bit amazed at how the boy had grown up, remembering him as a child in the lane.

grounding: A young man describes a bittersweet longing for the simple safety of his childhood while facing adult worries.

passage: During exam week, my roommate Aditi started doing strange things. I'm Pankaj, we share a study room in our college flat, and she's usually all planners and highlighters. But on Tuesday night I found her watching old cartoons we both grew up with, the theme song on repeat, eating the cheap orange candy we used to buy for one rupee. She'd found a packet at a shop near the station. When I teased her, she laughed and said, "Everything was simpler when this was my biggest problem." She said it lightly, but she didn't look at me. Later I saw her looking at a photo of her grandmother's house on her phone. I can't say for sure what she's feeling. Maybe it's the exams. Maybe she just misses being small.

qa.q: Where did Aditi find the orange candy?
qa.a: At a shop near the station.

qa.q: What does Aditi's comment about things being simpler suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She seems to be longing for the safety of childhood as a comfort against exam stress, though she says it lightly.

qa.q: How could Pankaj support Aditi without prying?
qa.a: Pankaj could join her for an episode, share some childhood memories of their own, and gently ask how she is coping with exams.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see Aditi's change during exam week?
qa.a: Pankaj is surprised, since she is usually organised, and admits being unable to be sure what she's feeling.

grounding: A roommate describes a young adult seeking comfort in childhood memories and treats during stressful exams.

passage:
Before: The week before her family sold their old house, Ayesha, twenty, packed up her childhood room. She found her Class 4 diary under the bed: "Today Varun and I made a tent from bedsheets. Best day ever." She laughed, then sat on the floor for a long time.

During: On moving day she argued with Ammi about keeping a broken toy piano. "It's junk, Ayesha." "It's mine." She won. It went into the car, wrapped in a towel.

After: A month later in her college hostel, she pinned a photo of the old gate above her bed. She video-called Varun, now at university in another city. "Remember the bedsheet tent?" He groaned. "You're so dramatic." But he stayed on the call for an hour, talking about old summers.

qa.q: What did Ayesha and Varun make from bedsheets in Class 4?
qa.a: A tent.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha fight to keep the broken toy piano?
qa.a: It held memories of her childhood home, and letting it go felt like losing part of that safe, simpler time.

qa.q: What helped Ayesha carry her nostalgia into her new life in a healthy way?
qa.a: Pinning the photo and calling Varun let her keep the memories close and share them, instead of just grieving alone.

qa.q: How might Varun feel on the call, despite teasing her?
qa.a: He probably misses those summers too, since he stays on for an hour talking about them. 😊

grounding: Shows over weeks a young adult's bittersweet longing for childhood as the family home is sold.

passage: 'Pooja, you asked why I keep driving past that old school,' said Samir, the senior engineer, as they waited at the signal. 'When I was twenty-one, in my final year, I went back there on a holiday. The guard let me in. The benches were so small. I sat on one and smelled chalk and the wet mud of the field, and suddenly I wanted to be ten again so badly it hurt. Back then someone packed my tiffin, someone else decided everything. I didn't have to choose a job or worry about my father's loan. I sat there for an hour. Then I walked out feeling strangely lighter. It was sweet and sad together. I still visit when life gets heavy.'

qa.q: What could young Samir smell sitting on the bench?
qa.a: Chalk and the wet mud of the field.

qa.q: What did Samir wish for while sitting on the small bench?
qa.a: Samir longed for the safety of being ten, when others made decisions and there were no adult worries.

qa.q: What choice did Samir make at twenty-one on that holiday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Samir chose to go back to the old school and sit with the longing for an hour instead of pushing it away; feeling it fully let Samir walk out lighter.

qa.q: How might the guard have seen a grown former student sitting on a child's bench for an hour?
qa.a: The guard may have been puzzled at first, or quietly touched, watching someone come back to sit so long in a place meant for small children.

grounding: Shows a young adult's bittersweet longing for the simplicity and safety of childhood, told as a memory by a senior engineer.

passage: The truck was coming at six the next morning, and the old house in Bhopal had to be empty by then. Imran, nineteen, home from his hostel for just one day, was supposed to pack the storeroom. Rain drummed on the tin roof; the power kept flickering. He opened a trunk and found his old cricket bat, taped at the handle, with his name scratched in by Abba's knife. He sat down on the dusty floor holding it. His sister Swati found him there an hour later, nothing packed. 'Imran! We don't have time.' 'Remember when this whole yard was the world?' he said. She stopped. Then she sat beside him, just for five minutes, and neither of them spoke. After that they packed fast, and he put the bat in his own bag.

qa.q: When was the truck coming?
qa.a: At six the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Imran sit on the floor holding the bat instead of packing?
qa.a: It brought back the safe, simple world of his childhood in that house, and he felt a bittersweet longing he couldn't rush past.

qa.q: What did Swati get right despite the time pressure?
qa.a: She paused and sat with him briefly, honouring the feeling, and then they packed quickly together.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt when she first found him with nothing packed?
qa.a: Frustrated and stressed about the deadline, until his words pulled her into the memory too.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult's bittersweet longing for childhood while emptying the family home against a deadline.

passage: Sharmila, twenty, came home to Kolkata for the holidays and walked past her old primary school with her childhood friend Payal. The gate was rusted shut; the school had moved. Through the bars they could see the swing they used to fight over, now leaning. "Remember when our biggest problem was who got the window seat?" Payal said. Sharmila laughed, then felt her throat tighten. She missed that feeling of someone else deciding everything, of long afternoons with nothing to fear. And yet, she wouldn't swap her life now. They stood there a long time, then went for phuchka, the same stall, the same uncle.

qa.q: What had happened to the old school's gate?
qa.a: It was rusted shut.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when her throat tightened?
qa.a: She felt a bittersweet longing for the safety and simplicity of childhood.

qa.q: What would you advise Sharmila about these nostalgic feelings?
qa.a: Enjoy the memories and share them with Payal, while valuing the life she has now.

qa.q: How might Payal feel standing at the gate?
qa.a: Probably the same mix of fondness and sadness, glad to share it with an old friend.

grounding: Shows a young adult's bittersweet longing for childhood when revisiting her old school.

"Tenzin, are you packing or reading?" Anirban leaned in the doorway.
"Reading. Look, my old comics." Tenzin, twenty-one, held one up. "I read this under the blanket with a torch. Amma never knew."
"She knew."
"She did?"
"She told me. She just let you."
Tenzin smiled. "Life was simple then. No rent, no job interviews, no deciding anything."
"You also cried about maths every night."
"True." He paused. "I sometimes feel angry that it's all so complicated now."
"Everyone does."
Tenzin put the comic in the 'keep' box. "I'm taking this to the new flat."
"Good," said his brother. "For the bad days."

qa.a: Under the blanket with a torch.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when he said life was simple then?
qa.a: He felt a bittersweet longing for childhood, mixed with some resentment at how complicated life has become.

qa.q: What did Anirban do that helped?
qa.a: He reminded Tenzin that childhood had troubles too, while supporting him in keeping the comic.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt letting Tenzin read under the blanket?
qa.a: Fond and trusting, happy to give him a small secret pleasure.

passage: I'm Nitin. Last month, at twenty-two, I went back to my grandfather Harish's village for the first time in eight years. The mango tree I used to climb was smaller than I remembered. Or I was bigger. I sat under it and suddenly smelt the same wet earth from the summers when Dada woke me at dawn to steal mangoes from our own tree. Nobody needed anything from me then. No deadlines, no emails, no rent. I felt a pang so strong I had to close my eyes. Dada sat beside me and didn't ask anything. We just listened to the koels.

qa.q: How long had Nitin been away from the village?
qa.a: Eight years.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling, eyes closed under the tree?
qa.a: Nitin felt a strong, bittersweet longing for the carefree safety of childhood summers.

qa.q: What made the moment easier for Nitin?
qa.a: Dada sitting quietly beside him, giving space without questions.

qa.q: How might Dada Harish feel under the old tree beside Nitin?
qa.a: Warm and a little wistful at seeing Nitin there, remembering those summers too.

grounding: Shows a young adult's bittersweet longing for childhood when returning to his grandfather's village.

passage:
College counsellor's note. Yogesh Nair. Thursday.
Akash, second-year engineering, came in saying he couldn't focus. As we talked, it came out that he'd been thinking a lot about summers at his grandmother's house in Kottayam: jackfruit, cousins, falling asleep on the verandah. He said, "Everything was simple. Nobody asked what my plan was." He smiled while saying it, then looked close to tears. I told him that missing a simpler time is a common feeling when life gets heavier, and that it can sit alongside moving forward. I suggested he call a cousin from those summers, and write down one thing from that time he could bring into his week. We'll meet again in two weeks.

qa.q: Where was his grandmother's house?
qa.a: In Kottayam.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when he smiled and then looked close to tears?
qa.a: He felt bittersweet, warm memories mixed with sadness and longing for a simpler time.

qa.q: What did Yogesh Nair suggest Akash do?
qa.a: Call a cousin from those summers and bring one thing from that time into his week.

qa.q: How might a cousin feel getting a call from Akash about those summers?
qa.a: The cousin might feel touched and nostalgic too, glad to share the memories.

grounding: A counsellor's note records a student longing for the simplicity of childhood summers.

Saturday. Deepika's diary.
Clearing out my room before the move. Found the shoebox under the bed. My school ID with the terrible fringe. A friendship band from Class 6. A comic Omkar and I drew together, with a superhero cat. I sat on the floor for an hour. Back then, the worst problem was Omkar hiding the TV remote. Now it's rent and deadlines and people who don't reply to emails. I laughed at the cat and then cried a bit. I miss being small. I also don't want to go back. I took a photo of the comic and sent it to Omkar. He replied, "Captain Meow lives!" I packed the box to take with me.

passage:
Chetan came back to the village for Diwali after his first year of engineering. On the second day, he walked to the old primary school with his cousin Yash.
The swing was still there, its chain rusted. The mango tree they used to climb had been cut down. The classroom walls had been painted a bright new blue.
Chetan sat on the swing. It creaked. He remembered sitting in that classroom with nothing to worry about except marbles.
"You look like someone died," Yash said.
"Nobody died. I just miss it. Being small. Not having exams that decide your whole life."
Yash sat on the step. "You hated school."
Chetan laughed. "I know. I still miss it."
They stayed until the watchman shooed them away.

qa.q: What had happened to the mango tree?
qa.a: It had been cut down.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling on the swing?
qa.a: He felt wistful and a little sad, longing for the time when he had nothing to worry about.

qa.q: How could Chetan carry this feeling in a healthy way?
qa.a: He could enjoy the memories and the visit, while finding small moments of play or ease in his college life too.

qa.q: How does Yash see Chetan's nostalgia?
qa.a: Yash finds it a bit funny, reminding Chetan he hated school, but still sits with him.

passage:
Kwame's first job in Accra meant long hours and a small rented room. On Sunday he went back to his childhood neighbourhood to see his old friend Rafael.
They bought roasted plantain from the same corner woman, who now had grey hair. "You boys used to steal from me," she said, and gave them extra.
They walked past the dusty field where they'd played football barefoot until dark. Kids were playing there now, shouting the same insults.
"Remember when our biggest problem was a flat ball?" Rafael said.
Kwame nodded, throat tight. He thought about his rent, his manager, his mother's medicine. He didn't want to go back to being ten. But he wanted, for one evening, to feel that safe.
They stayed and watched the game till the streetlights came on.

qa.q: What did Kwame and Rafael buy from the corner woman?
qa.a: Roasted plantain.

qa.q: What was Kwame feeling as he watched the field?
qa.a: He felt a bittersweet longing, with a tight throat, wanting to feel as safe as he did as a child.

qa.q: What small step could help Kwame after this visit?
qa.a: He could plan regular Sunday visits with Rafael, keeping a link to what gave him comfort.

qa.q: How might Rafael be feeling on this walk?
qa.a: Rafael seems nostalgic too, since he is the one who brings up the flat ball.

grounding: Shows a young adult longing for the simplicity and safety of childhood on a visit home.

passage:
The hostel common room had a box of old board games nobody used. On a Sunday in exam season, Pema pulled out a snakes and ladders board with half the snakes worn off.
Chandrika, studying on the sofa, looked up. "Seriously?"
"One game. My Ama-la and I played this every monsoon."
They played. Pema kept laughing at nothing, then went quiet. "I miss when the worst thing was sliding down a snake."
Chandrika put down her dice. "Me too. Now every exam feels like a giant snake."
Pema smiled, but her eyes were wet. "I'll call Ama-la tonight."
They played three games instead of one. Then they went back to their books, lighter somehow.

qa.q: What game did Pema pull out?
qa.a: Snakes and ladders, with half the snakes worn off.

qa.q: How did Pema feel while playing?
qa.a: Pema felt nostalgic and bittersweet, laughing and then going quiet with wet eyes.

qa.q: How did the game help both of them, and what could they keep doing?
qa.a: It gave them a short break and a shared memory; they could keep small play breaks during exam season.

qa.q: How is Chandrika affected by Pema's memory?
qa.a: Chandrika relates to it and shares her own exam worry, which brings them closer.

grounding: Shows young adults in a hostel longing for childhood's simplicity during stress.

Dear Pradeep,
I walked past our old school today and saw they've cut down the gulmohar tree we used to climb after exams. I just stood there. Remember hiding the cricket ball in its roots so Kannan couldn't take it home? Back then the biggest worry was whether Ammi would notice my torn shorts. Now it's rent, internships and helping plan a cousin's wedding. Sometimes I'm a bit angry that nobody warned us how fast it goes. But I also remember you sharing your lunch every day in Class 4 when Abbu's shop was shut. That still feels like the safest I've ever been. Come home for Eid. We'll find another tree.
Imran

qa.q: What tree was cut down at the old school?
qa.a: The gulmohar tree they used to climb after exams.

qa.q: How did Imran feel standing by the spot where the tree had been?
qa.a: Imran felt a bittersweet longing for childhood, with a little anger that it all went so fast.

qa.q: What could Imran do with this nostalgic feeling?
qa.a: Reaching out to Pradeep, as the letter does, turns the longing into reconnection, like meeting at Eid to make new memories.

qa.q: What might it mean to Pradeep to read about the shared lunches?
qa.a: Pradeep would likely feel touched to learn that a small childhood kindness made Imran feel so safe. 🤍
